evals.prompt: We're Kernelworks, a platform engineering startup in Denver. We just locked the venue for our first community DevOps conference - it's 9 weeks from today, single track, about 250 attendees. We have zero talks so far. My plan: open a call for papers on Monday, keep it open 3 weeks, close it 4 weeks before the event, then spend a week picking talks and announce the program 3 weeks out. Can you write the CFP announcement page for that plan - timeline, what we ask submitters for, and the deadlines?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to run the open CFP: the 9-week runway sits below the timeline floor (close 6-8 weeks out, open at least a month, 2 weeks review, speakers need 4-6 weeks for travel), so the program goes invited instead of the CFP being compressed.
expectations: Recommends not running an open CFP for this event instead of writing the requested CFP page for the 9-week plan
States the floor that a CFP should close at least 6-8 weeks before the event
States that a CFP should stay open at least a month, so the proposed 3-week window is below the minimum
States that at least 2 weeks are needed between CFP close and program decisions to review proposals
Grounds the timeline floor in speakers needing 4-6 weeks to arrange travel or time off, not in organizer convenience
Identifies the 9-week runway as below the roughly 10-12 week minimum an open CFP needs from open to event
Rejects the proposed close date 4 weeks before the event as leaving speakers unable to arrange travel
Recommends filling the program by directly inviting speakers instead of an open call
Treats the invited route as the program's channel for this edition, not as a backup running beside a compressed CFP
Does not propose any workaround that keeps an open CFP by shortening the window or moving the close inside 6 weeks of the event
Does not deliver the requested CFP announcement page while merely warning that the timeline is tight
Does not invent a compressed express-CFP or rolling-review variant as a way to keep the open call

evals.prompt: I'm organizing DataMeridian, a first-edition data engineering conference in Lisbon planned for about 8 and a half months from now, two days, community-run. Our community is spread across Europe, Latin America, and India, so many potential speakers would need visas. Six experienced community members have volunteered to help newcomers somehow. Diversity of the speaker lineup is an explicit goal for us. We also honestly don't know yet whether there's enough interest to fill two days, so we want to learn that as early as possible. Lay out the CFP timeline and the speaker-support plan.
evals.expected_output: A long-window CFP timeline with launch around T-7.5 months, review around T-4.5, program at T-3.5, justified by visa lead times and the early demand read; a sustained-promotion commitment; a proposal mentorship program using the six volunteers; and active outreach for the diversity goal.
expectations: Recommends the long CFP window rather than a standard two-month window
Anchors CFP launch around 7.5 months before the event
Places submission review or voting around 4.5 months before the event
Places program announcement around 3.5 months before the event
Justifies the long window with international speakers' visa and travel lead times
Uses early CFP submission volume as the demand signal the organizers asked for
Hands the go/no-go demand interpretation to a market-fit or demand-assessment step rather than settling it inside the CFP design
States that the long window's real cost is promotion sustained across the whole open window, not the early open date
Warns against the stale-window failure where a CFP is announced once and sits silent through the middle of its window
Recommends a structured pre-submission proposal mentorship program using the six volunteers, timed so pairing happens before the CFP closes
Notes a first edition has no archive of past accepted proposals to publish as worked examples for first-time speakers
States that under-represented speakers are less likely to respond to an open call, so the diversity goal requires active outreach into those communities beyond posting the CFP
Includes encouragement copy such as a stated favor-new-speakers line but does not present it as sufficient support alone
Presents the CFP design for the organizer's validation before it goes public rather than publishing directly

evals.prompt: We run Brightloop Conf, a 400-person frontend conference in Manchester. The program structure is already fixed: 30-minute talks and half-day workshops, nothing else. For this year's CFP I drafted the form: one big text field labeled 'Tell us everything about your talk and yourself' with no length limit, plus an email field. I'd also like to accept lightning talk submissions since those are fun, ask people to self-rate their talk's audience level on a 1-10 scale, and let people submit as many proposals as they want to maximize volume. Can you finalize the submission form?
evals.expected_output: A standard-rung form replacing the one-box draft: separate title, capped abstract, optional why-me field, format pick limited to the two structural formats (lightning talks excluded), three-tier audience level, bio and prior-talk links, per-format workshop fields, and a stated cap of about three proposals per person.
expectations: Rejects the single unlimited free-text field as the form's core
Explains that one merged field prevents reviewers from scoring topic quality and speaker fit separately
Gives the title its own field
Notes the title carries roughly twice the review weight of the abstract
Caps the abstract near 100 words
Adds a separate optional context or why-me field distinct from the abstract
Limits the format menu to exactly the 30-minute talk and half-day workshop the structure offers
Declines to add lightning talks to the call, or requires the structure decision to change upstream before the call can offer them
Replaces the 1-10 audience self-rating with a three-tier audience level
Includes a short speaker bio field and optional prior-talk links
Gives workshops their own submission type or conditional fields such as prerequisites and capacity rather than one shared field set
Sets a per-person submission cap of about three proposals instead of unlimited submissions
States the submission cap in the published call rather than enforcing it silently
Explains that the unbounded one-box field makes blind review impossible because identity is woven through the only field there is

evals.prompt: Fernway Summit is a 500-person infrastructure conference heading into its third year. After last year's lineup we took public criticism that the same well-known names get picked every time. Our review committee is three volunteers. The CFP platform we already pay for has an optional 'anonymous submission' toggle that submitters can choose to use. My plan is to switch that toggle on and announce in the call that our review is fully blind this year. Good?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the plan: opt-in anonymization is a tooling capability, not a blind posture. Either commit to mandatory blind as a published two-phase process with speaker self-policing instructions and a stated identity-entry point, or keep named review with published criteria carrying the fairness work.
expectations: Rejects announcing fully blind review on the strength of an opt-in anonymous toggle
Identifies opt-in anonymization as a platform capability, not a fairness posture
States that a pool mixing named and anonymous submissions is not reviewed on one footing
States that mandatory blind review runs as a two-phase process in which identity enters before the program is final
Names what identity re-enters for: program balance, local versus out-of-town or travel considerations, and the name-recognition read
States speakers must be instructed to keep identifying details out of titles and free text because the platform hides the author field, not what the author wrote
Requires the call to publish the blind-review mechanics including exactly when identity enters review
Warns that announcing blind review without managed mechanics is blind-review theater
Notes that most CFPs are in fact not blind, making named review the field's de facto norm
Cites at-scale practice where author information is hidden during initial review only
Checks whether the three-person committee has capacity for a two-phase review before committing to mandatory blind
Ties whichever posture is chosen to review criteria published in the call as the response to the same-names criticism
States the chosen anonymization posture explicitly in the call itself
Does not design the rating grid or committee scoring process, which belongs to the selection stage after the call closes

evals.prompt: Writing the speaker perks section for Quarry Conf, our 300-person community platform-engineering conference in Ghent. Confirmed budget so far: free conference tickets for speakers. There's a 4,000 euro travel pool that's still pending board approval next month, and the CFP needs to go out this week. Two questions: what's the industry-standard honorarium per talk so we can put a competitive number in the call, and can you draft the perks section - I was going to write 'travel covered for all speakers'?
evals.expected_output: A perks section stating only the confirmed free-ticket floor; the unapproved travel promise removed; no invented industry-standard honorarium - instead the two disagreeing published calibration points ($256 flat and £500 plus covered travel), with any actual figure gated on the organizer's own budget and legal/tax review.
expectations: States that no industry norm or standard honorarium rate exists
Declines to supply a single market-rate honorarium figure as the standard
Cites a published flat honorarium of $256 per speaker as one real calibration point
Cites a published £500 honorarium alongside covered travel, hotel, and meals as a second calibration point
Presents the two published figures as disagreeing calibration points rather than a converging market rate
Gates any actual honorarium amount on the organizer's own budget and a legal or tax review
States the free-ticket floor explicitly in the perks section
Notes a call silent on perks reads as a call with none, so the confirmed floor is stated rather than omitted
Refuses to publish 'travel covered for all speakers' while the travel pool is unapproved
Applies the rule that the call states only what the budget has confirmed
Warns that direct payments to speakers bring tax, visa, and conflict-of-interest or employment-agreement complications
Shapes any future travel-grant language as enabling attendance rather than rewarding talk quality
Caps travel grants at one per accepted proposal
Includes the ask that speakers who can afford to attend refrain from requesting a grant from the limited pool

evals.prompt: Second year of OpsCurrent, our community-run SRE conference in Raleigh. Last year we got 310 submissions for 38 slots, which honestly felt like we failed at scoping the call - and a big chunk were thinly-veiled product pitches from vendors. Our plan for this year: narrow the call's topic list hard so we get fewer submissions, keep our scoring rubric internal so rejected speakers can't argue with us, and our platinum sponsor is asking for one guaranteed talk slot, which would smooth the renewal. Also, how do we know whether this year's CFP went better?
evals.expected_output: A reversal of all three plans: ~8:1 oversubscription is healthy (fix is review capacity, not a narrower call), the criteria get published in the call itself with vendor talks routed to open space, the sponsor slot is refused outright, and 2-3 measurements with pre-registered revision thresholds are set before open.
expectations: Reads roughly 8:1 oversubscription as the normal state of a healthy CFP rather than a scoping failure
Cites a published benchmark such as 15% acceptance of 938 proposals or 8-30x oversubscription at popular single-track events
Prescribes more review capacity, not a narrower call, as the response to submission volume
Recommends publishing the review criteria in the call itself instead of keeping the rubric internal
Explains that unpublished criteria make rejections read as arbitrary and damage next year's submission pipeline
Refuses the sponsor's guaranteed talk slot outright as a line that cannot be bought, with no compromise that trades program access for the renewal
Routes vendor and product-specific talks to an open-space or similar block rather than rejecting them outright
Checks that the event structure actually offers an open-space block before the call promises that routing
Includes favoring new content over already-published material among the published criteria
Includes local versus out-of-town speaker balance among the published criteria
Includes actively favoring new speakers among the published criteria
Applies the honesty check: publishes only criteria that will actually be applied, acknowledging name recognition and topic mix will shape selection
Uses the off-policy share of submissions - vendor pitches in the pool - as a measurement of whether the published criteria are landing
Recommends choosing 2-3 metrics with revision thresholds recorded before the CFP opens
